title: Wittgenstein's Tractarian Ontology
description: A Lean 4 formalization of the structural core of Wittgenstein's Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus: objects, states of affairs, worlds, propositions, truth-functionality, and first-order quantifiers. Proves compositionality for both propositional and first-order languages. Extends to HOAS-encoded quantifiers with duality and distribution theorems. Ends with a deliberate axiom — the silence of Proposition 7.

mathlibDependencies.description: Law of excluded middle (classical logic axiom)

originalContributions: Formal ontology mapping Tractatus propositions to Lean types
Truth-functional compositionality theorem via structural induction
Elementary independence theorem witnessing the Sachverhalt/world correspondence
First-order extension using HOAS (higher-order abstract syntax) for quantifier binding
Compositionality extended to first-order propositions with quantifiers
Universal-existential duality and distribution theorems for the extended language
Philosophical annotations bridging formal verification and Wittgensteinian philosophy
meta.assumptions: One deliberate axiom: `silence : True` (TLP 7) — a trivially true but axiomatic declaration that enacts Wittgenstein's silence as a formal gesture. All theorems are fully proved with 0 sorries. Uses classical logic (Classical.em) throughout. The companion file TractatusQuantifiers.lean has no sorries or axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) is Wittgenstein's only book-length philosophical work published in his lifetime. It presents a logical atomist ontology: the world consists of facts (obtaining states of affairs), propositions picture possible states of affairs, and all meaningful propositions are truth-functions of elementary propositions. The work culminates in proposition 6.54 — the famous ladder that must be thrown away — and the closing injunction: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.'
overview.problemStatement: Can the structural core of the Tractatus — its ontology of objects, states of affairs, worlds, truth-functional propositions, and quantifiers — be faithfully formalized in a modern proof assistant? What is captured by formalization, and what necessarily escapes?
overview.proofStrategy: We define types for objects (opaque), states of affairs (abstract), and worlds (predicates on states of affairs). Propositions form an inductive type with elementary, negation, and conjunction constructors. All other connectives are derived. A recursive evaluation function maps propositions to truth values relative to worlds. We then extend to first-order propositions (FOProp) using higher-order abstract syntax (HOAS) for quantifier binding, and prove compositionality, duality, and distribution theorems for the extended language.
keyInsights: The world-as-predicate encoding makes elementary independence trivially true — the assignment IS the world
Truth-functional compositionality follows by structural induction on the proposition type
HOAS encoding of quantifiers allows Lean's structural recursion to handle first-order evaluation without explicit substitution or de Bruijn indices
The formalization necessarily works at the metalevel — we prove theorems ABOUT propositions in Lean, which is precisely the kind of thing Wittgenstein says can only be shown, not said
Classical logic (excluded middle) is used throughout, matching Wittgenstein's bivalent semantics
prerequisites: Familiarity with Lean 4 syntax (inductive types, pattern matching)
Some acquaintance with the Tractatus is helpful but not required

sections.title: Preamble and Design Decisions
sections.summary: Module imports, documentation header, and Design Decisions block documenting six load-bearing modeling choices (worlds as predicates, independence by construction, classical logic, HOAS quantifiers, abstract types, axiomatic silence).

sections.title: TLP 1-2.06: Objects and States of Affairs
sections.summary: Objects as an abstract variable type — simple, structureless entities.

sections.title: TLP 2.01-2.062: States of Affairs (Sachverhalte)
sections.summary: States of affairs (Sachverhalte) as an abstract type of possible combinations.

sections.title: TLP 2.1-2.174: Worlds as Predicates
sections.summary: Worlds as predicates determining which states of affairs obtain.

sections.title: TLP 4.2-4.463: Propositions and Logical Space
sections.summary: Inductive type for propositions: elementary, negation, conjunction.

sections.title: TLP 5: Truth-Functionality (Formalized)
sections.summary: Disjunction, implication, biconditional, and NAND defined from negation and conjunction.

sections.title: TLP 5.1-5.14: Semantic Evaluation
sections.summary: Recursive truth-value evaluation of propositions relative to worlds, including Bool-valued evaluator and correctness bridge.

sections.title: TLP 5.502: Tautology and Contradiction
sections.summary: Definitions of tautology (true in all worlds) and contradiction (false in all worlds).

sections.title: TLP 6.1: Core Theorems
sections.summary: Fifteen theorems establishing compositionality, independence, bivalence, connective semantics, and functional completeness.

sections.title: Concrete Examples (TwoFacts Instantiation)
sections.summary: Instantiates the abstract Sachverhalt type with a two-element concrete type (rain and snow), demonstrating both Prop-valued and Bool-valued evaluation with #eval.

sections.title: TLP 6.54-7: Limits of Formalization
sections.summary: Closing philosophical reflection on what escapes formalization — the ladder, the silence, and the formal content of TLP 7.

conclusion.summary: We have formalized the ontological skeleton of the Tractatus: objects, states of affairs, worlds, and truth-functional propositions. Sixteen theorems are fully proved; the seventeenth — that inexpressible truths exist — is stated and deliberately left as sorry. The silence of Proposition 7 is enacted, not just cited.
conclusion.implications: This demonstrates that the formal core of the Tractatus — often dismissed as merely philosophical rather than mathematical — admits precise statement and machine-verified proof. The exercise also reveals where formalization reaches its limits: the saying/showing distinction, the nature of logical form, and the self-undermining character of 6.54 all resist capture in any formal system.
openQuestions: Could dependent types better capture TLP 2.0141 — that an object's form IS its combinatorial possibility?
Is there a formalization that captures the saying/showing distinction without collapsing it?
How does this propositional framework relate to Wittgenstein's later rejection of logical atomism?
Can the N-operator connection (TLP 5.52) be made precise for infinite domains, or is Geach (1981) correct that it fails?
Does the HOAS encoding faithfully capture the Tractarian view of variables, or does it import too much metatheory?

references.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.note: Translated by C.K. Ogden and F.P. Ramsey. The numbering system (1, 1.1, 2.01, etc.) indicates logical dependencies between propositions.

references.title: Introduction to the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.note: Russell's introduction — which Wittgenstein reportedly disliked — interprets the Tractatus within the framework of Principia Mathematica.

references.title: A set of five independent postulates for Boolean algebras
references.venue: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 14
references.note: Introduces the Sheffer stroke (NAND), which Wittgenstein references in TLP 5.5 as showing all truth-functions reduce to a single operation.

references.title: Wittgenstein's Operator N
references.note: Argues that Wittgenstein's N-operator cannot handle all quantified propositions as claimed in TLP 5.52, particularly for infinite domains.

references.title: Generality, Truth-Functions, and Expressive Capacity in the Tractatus
references.note: Shows that the claim that all propositions are truth-functions of elementary propositions (TLP 5) is undermined by the infinite-domain case of quantification.

additionalFiles.description: First-order extension: FOProp type with HOAS quantifiers, evaluation, compositionality, duality, and distribution theorems (TLP 5.52, 5.521, 5.526)

mainTheorems.name: tautology_is_world_invariant
mainTheorems.description: A proposition is a tautology iff it holds in every world (TLP 6.1)
mainTheorems.leanType: (∀ w : World S, p.eval w) ↔ IsTautology p

mainTheorems.name: truth_functional_compositionality
mainTheorems.description: Worlds agreeing on elementaries agree on all compounds (TLP 5)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (p : Proposition S) (w₁ w₂ : World S), (∀ s, w₁ s ↔ w₂ s) → (p.eval w₁ ↔ p.eval w₂)

mainTheorems.name: elementary_independence
mainTheorems.description: Any truth-value assignment to states of affairs is realizable (TLP 2.061)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∃ w : World S, ∀ s : S, w s ↔ assignment s

mainTheorems.name: excluded_middle_tautology
mainTheorems.description: p ∨ ¬p is a tautology — paradigmatic logical truth (TLP 4.46)

mainTheorems.name: truth_functional_compositionality_fo
mainTheorems.description: Worlds agreeing on elementaries agree on all first-order compounds including quantifiers (TLP 5, extended)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (p : FOProp S D) (w₁ w₂ : World S), (∀ s, w₁ s ↔ w₂ s) → (p.eval w₁ ↔ p.eval w₂)

mainTheorems.name: forall_exists_duality
mainTheorems.leanType: (FOProp.negFO (FOProp.forall_ (fun d => FOProp.negFO (f d)))).eval w ↔ (FOProp.exists_ f).eval w

mainTheorems.name: forall_distrib_conj
mainTheorems.leanType: (FOProp.forall_ (fun d => FOProp.conjFO (f d) (g d))).eval w ↔ (FOProp.conjFO (FOProp.forall_ f) (FOProp.forall_ g)).eval w
